turns.text: What's the deal with Chromebooks? / Are they any good?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're great for simple things, browsing, email, documents, video. They're cheap and they start up really fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can they run regular programs?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mostly they run web apps and Android apps. Big programs like professional photo editors usually won't work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My mum just does email and watches cooking videos.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a Chromebook is perfect for her. Simple, secure, and hard to break with a wrong click.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it get viruses?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very rarely. That's one of their big advantages, especially for less techy users.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm left handed and I hate trackpads. Any laptop tips?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Plenty of left handed people use a mouse, honestly. A small wireless mouse fixes most trackpad frustration.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Even on the go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, there are tiny travel mice that fit in a pocket. Some fold flat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are there laptops with better trackpads at least?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some have bigger, smoother glass trackpads that feel much nicer. Try a few in a store if you can.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And keyboards? / Anything specific for left handers?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not really, but a laptop with a number pad shifts the keyboard to the left, which some lefties actually like.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does refresh rate mean on a laptop screen?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's how many times per second the screen updates. Higher means smoother motion, especially when scrolling or gaming.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need a high one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you game, a hundred and twenty or more feels great. For office work and browsing, sixty is fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it drain the battery?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A bit, yes. Many laptops let you switch it down when you're on battery.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I mostly watch shows and do spreadsheets.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then don't pay extra for it. Put the money into a brighter, sharper screen instead.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My laptop keeps overheating. Should I just buy a new one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not necessarily. Overheating is often just dust in the fans. Have you ever cleaned it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Never. It's four years old.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a cleaning could make a big difference. A repair shop can do it cheaply if you don't want to open it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything else I can do?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use it on a hard surface, not a bed or a couch. A cheap cooling pad can help too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if that doesn't work?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it might be the thermal paste drying out. A shop can replace it, it's still way cheaper than a new laptop.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm thinking of buying a laptop online but I'm scared of getting a dud.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's fair. Buying from a big retailer or the brand directly makes returns a lot easier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long do I usually have to return it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often fourteen to thirty days. Check before you buy, and keep the box and all the bits.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should I check when it arrives?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for dead pixels, test the keyboard and ports, and run it for a few hours to see how it handles heat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, that sounds / doable, actually.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. And if anything feels off, start the return quickly. Don't wait until the last day.

option_sets.lead_in: I need help picking a laptop for school.
options: The first one is a really thin laptop, very light, great battery, but only eight gigs of memory.
Then there's a gaming laptop that's super powerful, but it's heavy and the battery lasts maybe three hours.
And the last one is a basic model, cheaper than the others, with a slightly dim screen.
moshi_comment: For school, the thin laptop sounds like the best fit, since you'll carry it around and need the battery to last through classes. The gaming laptop only makes sense if you'll actually game or run heavy software. The basic model is fine if budget is the main concern.

Do you play games or use any demanding programs for your classes? If not, I'd go with the thin one, eight gigs is enough for notes and browsing. The gaming laptop's short battery would be a real pain on campus.

option_sets.lead_in: My mom wants a new laptop and asked me to help her decide.
options: One is a simple Chromebook that's cheap and easy, mostly for email and video calls.
Another is a regular Windows laptop with a big screen, which is what she's used to.
Or there's a tablet with a keyboard cover, smaller but really easy to carry around.
moshi_comment: If she mostly does email and video calls, the Chromebook is simple and hard to mess up. The Windows laptop is familiar, which really matters for some people. The tablet is handy, but typing long emails on it can be a little cramped.

I'd lean toward the Windows laptop with the big screen, since familiar and easy to read is a big deal. Does she need any special programs, or is it really just email and calls? If it's just those, the Chromebook would save money.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm a freelance writer and I need help picking a new laptop.
options: A small light laptop with an amazing keyboard and eighteen hours of battery, but a fairly dim screen.
A two in one with a pen and a touchscreen, nice for notes, but the keyboard is a bit shallow.
A big fifteen inch one with a great screen and number pad, though it weighs over two kilos.
moshi_comment: For a writer, the keyboard and battery of the small one are hard to beat, the dim screen matters less indoors. The two in one is fun but a shallow keyboard gets tiring. The big one is great at a desk, but heavy if you work in cafes.

I'd pick the small light one, it's built for long writing days. If you take a lot of handwritten notes, the two in one could be worth a look. The big one only makes sense if you rarely leave your desk.

option_sets.lead_in: My nephew is starting engineering and his parents want my advice on a laptop.
options: A powerful workstation laptop with a strong graphics card, which handles design software but costs nearly two thousand.
A mid range laptop with good memory, decent graphics, about nine hundred, and a little heavy.
A cheap thin laptop for notes and emails, with him using the university's computer labs for heavy work.
moshi_comment: Engineering software can be demanding, so the cheap one might leave him stuck in the labs late at night. The workstation is great but probably overkill for first year. The mid range one sounds like the sweet spot.

I'd go with the mid range laptop, it handles most first year software and costs half the workstation. Check the course's recommended specs before buying, though. The cheap option only works if the labs are really accessible.

option_sets.lead_in: I play music and I'm looking for a laptop for recording at home.
options: A Mac with a fast chip and a silent fan, which is great for music apps but pricey to upgrade storage.
A Windows laptop with lots of ports and a big drive, cheaper, though the fan gets loud under load.
A secondhand pro laptop from a friend, two years old, very powerful, but no warranty at all.
moshi_comment: For recording, a silent machine is a big deal, so the Mac has a real edge. The Windows laptop's loud fan could end up on your tracks. The secondhand one is tempting, as long as you trust your friend and test it well.

I'd lean toward the Mac, and use an external drive for storage to save money. The secondhand laptop could be a great deal if you can check it properly. The noisy fan on the Windows one worries me for recording.
